4 SHIFTS DEFINING THE NEXT ERA OF RETAIL — PREPARED FOR L.L.BEAN

L.L.Bean Rewards is ten weeks old. What it becomes is up for grabs.

A free loyalty program, a refreshed Mastercard, eight new store markets and a 114-year-old promise to treat customers like human beings. The gap between what members expect and what a promotions calendar can deliver has never been wider. These are the four shifts that close it — and how we'd workshop them with your team.

The four shifts

4 shifts defining the next era of L.L.Bean Rewards

Each shift is an area where retailers consistently leave value on the table. For L.L.Bean, each maps to something already in motion — a program launch, a card refresh, a store expansion, a platform investment. Together they form a loyalty strategy that compounds.

Shift 1

True 1:1 Personalization

Every member thinks they're your most important one. The shift is making that true — not just in marketing, but in every decision the brand makes.

At L.L.Bean: serve the heritage outdoorsperson and the lifestyle newcomer simultaneously — one decision per member, not one promo per segment.

Shift 2

Loyalty Built on Experience

Points and discounts buy transactions. The shift is from loyalty programs to loyalty moments — earned in real time, in the spaces between purchases.

At L.L.Bean: turn Rewards mechanics — 150-point thresholds, 270-day Bean Bucks expiry, Outdoor Impact votes — into individually timed moments.

Shift 3

Agentic Marketing Execution

Seasons change. Markets move. The shift is from slow, siloed campaign execution to a single decision layer that responds at the speed of now.

The AI Decisioning Brain

CDPs know who your customer is. The shift is adding the layer that decides what to do next, in real time, across every channel, with one set of rules.

Why this matters now

A promotions calendar can't operationalize the Golden Rule. A decision engine can.

“Sell good merchandise at a reasonable profit, treat your customers like human beings, and they will always come back for more.” At digital scale, that promise lives or dies in thousands of small choices a day: whether to send, what to offer, when to stay quiet.

Pega CDH positions loyalty promotions as a margin-protection and trust engine — not a discounting tool. Offers are arbitrated only where they measurably change behavior; at-risk members are caught 30–90 days before lapse; abandoned digital journeys are recovered without blanket incentives.
  • Reserve discounts for members and moments where they move behavior — defending compressed margins
  • Shift from “sell” to “service” mode automatically when a member shows churn risk or an open complaint
  • Recognize the same member in store, online, in the app, on the phone — with the same decision logic
  • Industry benchmarks: 20–40% lift in offer conversion, 5–15% abandoned-cart recovery, 3–5× ROI vs. segment campaigns
Illustrative: the same “members-only outerwear” budget, decided per member instead of per calendar slot.
Outside together

Members don't experience channels. They experience L.L.Bean.

A promotion that respects what a member did yesterday in a store, this morning on the app and ten minutes ago with customer service is the difference between a program people tolerate and one they value. That coordination is what a decisioning layer provides.

The proposed workshop

A half-day working session on L.L.Bean Rewards promotions

Not a demo. We bring the Pega Customer Engagement Blueprint and the Forrester TEI model; your team brings the Rewards roadmap, the promo calendar and the questions. We leave with three to five prioritized, quantified use cases.

1

Map the member moments

Walk the L.L.Bean Rewards and Mastercard lifecycles end to end — enrollment, earn, threshold, redeem, expiry, vote, upgrade, lapse — and mark where today's promotions fire by calendar instead of by signal.

2

Design the first decisions

Pick two or three moments and sketch them live in Blueprint: eligibility, arbitration between offer vs. service vs. silence, channel sequencing, fatigue rules, and what “success” looks like for each.

3

Size the value and the path

Adapt the TEI model to your member counts and spend, agree on the measurement design, and outline a packaged first release that fits alongside commercetools and Zipline — timed to the 2027 store openings.

SHIFT 1 OF 4 — TRUE 1:1 PERSONALIZATION

Every member thinks they're your most important one. Prove them right.

Most “personalization” is still segment-level guesswork — a promotion optimized for a cohort of 40,000, not the person standing at the Freeport counter. Pega CDH makes every decision at a true segment of one — which is how L.L.Bean can serve its heritage loyalists and its newest lifestyle customers without diluting either.

Schedule the loyalty workshop →Next: Loyalty →

For L.L.Bean, 1:1 means

  • Adaptive persona activation — a spectrum from legacy outdoorsperson to Gen Z tote buyer, re-scored on every interaction
  • Next-best-offer for complementary gear — boot care and wool socks after a boot purchase, consistently across web, app, phone and store
  • Made-in-Maine premium upsell for values-driven members who engage with sustainability content
  • B2B signal detection — surfacing L.L.Bean for Business to members showing bulk or corporate-gifting patterns
40K
People per typical segment

The average cohort size behind most retail “personalization” — a crowd, not a person.

2
Identities one member can hold

The same person can be a boot-and-flannel traditionalist in October and a kayak-curious newcomer in June. CDH scores both, every time, rather than filing them in one bucket.

+38%
Second-purchase conversion lift

What happens when the right message reaches the right person at exactly the right time.

Segmentation vs. personalization

Averaging your members destroys relevance for all of them

Two L.L.Bean members can share a segment — same region, comparable spend, both Rewards members since launch week. One bought Maine-made boots and reads every sustainability story you publish. The other arrived through a social campaign and hasn't opened an email in a month. A promotion that treats them the same fails both.

Why CDH is different Most vendors talk personalization but still act on segments. Pega evaluates every member, in context, immediately — detecting intent, hesitation and sentiment before any message fires.
  • Detects hesitation, price sensitivity and intent in real time — on llbean.com, in the app, at the register
  • Knows when to market, when to service, when to pause — or stay silent
  • Responds to current behavior, not past averages — and re-scores the persona on every interaction
  • Like your best Freeport associate reading the room — at the scale of every store and every session
Illustrative: the same member base, decided one person at a time.
Real-world scenario

In-store + digital: the associate who already knows

A Rewards member has been browsing technical rain shells on the app for three evenings. On Saturday she walks into the new Ann Arbor store — a market where L.L.Bean had no customers eight months ago. By the time she reaches an associate, CDH has already surfaced her browse history, her points position (118 of 150) and that she's never bought footwear.

Without CDH

The associate starts from zero. The app sends a generic “still thinking about it?” push on Sunday. Monday's members-only email offers 20% off… fleece. Three touches, zero coordination.

With CDH

The associate sees one recommendation: the shell she was comparing, plus a note that this purchase clears her first $5 in Bean Bucks. No discount is spent. The Sunday push is suppressed because the purchase happened. When associates know what members want, they sell more of it — in every store, every day, not just when the right person is on shift.

SHIFT 2 OF 4 — LOYALTY BUILT ON EXPERIENCE

Loyalty is won in the moments between purchases.

Points and Bean Bucks buy transactions. Experience builds loyalty. L.L.Bean Rewards already generates a rich stream of member moments — a points balance nearing 150, Bean Bucks about to expire, an Outdoor Impact vote waiting to be cast, a return that went sideways. CDH detects each one and decides, member by member, whether the right response is a promotion, a reminder, a thank-you, or silence.

Schedule the loyalty workshop →Next: Agentic Marketing →

Loyalty promotions we'd design together

  • Spend-to-threshold nudges — “you're $22 from $5 in Bean Bucks” — behavior-triggered, not calendar-triggered
  • Expiry rescue — Bean Bucks expire 270 days after the last earn; CDH times the reminder to the member, and only when a balance is at stake
  • Save journeys 30–90 days before lapse — a service gesture or personal outreach before a discount
  • Rewards → Mastercard progression — the 5%, birthday-bonus upgrade offered when it's suitable for that member, not to everyone
  • Values moments — Outdoor Impact Vote reminders and 10%-off Outdoor Discovery invites tied to what they actually bought
150 pts
= $5 in Bean Bucks

The core mechanic of L.L.Bean Rewards. Every member sits somewhere on the path to the next $5 — and that position is a decisioning signal most loyalty stacks never use.

270 days
Until Bean Bucks expire

Every unredeemed balance is a built-in re-engagement moment. The question is whether the reminder is a blast on day 240 or a 1:1 decision based on that member's rhythm.

~28%
Industry avg. second-purchase rate

Only ~28% of first-time buyers come back, and the window usually closes within 100 days — which makes Rewards enrollment at first purchase the highest-leverage moment in the program.

Industry benchmark
Retention & relationship

Proactive retention beats reactive win-back every time

Meta and Google consume the majority of retail acquisition budgets, and L.L.Bean is about to spend into eight markets at once. The path to profitable growth is keeping the members you already have — including the catalog loyalists and long-tenured customers whose relationship with the brand predates the app. That requires knowing when a relationship is at risk before it ends.

Why CDH is different CDH detects loyalty risk in the moment. When a member has a poor service experience, every downstream channel pivots to recovery mode — not sales mode — automatically, until trust signals recover.
  • Proactive save journeys 30–90 days before lapse replace expensive reactive win-back campaigns
  • Lead with a service gesture or personal outreach — reaffirming the promise — before reaching for a discount
  • Guide catalog-reliant members through a personalized path to phone-assisted and simplified digital ordering
  • Prove loyalty-promotion impact on lifetime value — not just opens, clicks and redemption counts
Illustrative: five Rewards signals, each resolved to one next best action per member.
Program mechanics as decisioning signals

L.L.Bean Rewards already produces the signals. CDH turns them into promotions that feel personal.

Launched August 11, the program is simple by design: 1 point per $1, 150 points to $5 in Bean Bucks, free shipping over $50, 10% off Outdoor Discovery Programs, and an Outdoor Impact Vote with every purchase. Each rule is also a moment a member can be helped toward — or left to miss.

  • Threshold nudges: trigger when a member is within one typical basket of 150 points — not on a fixed day
  • Expiry rescue: Bean Bucks lapse 270 days after the last earn event; CDH schedules the reminder to each member's cadence and suppresses it when nothing is at stake
  • Values moments: an unused Outdoor Impact Vote or a relevant Outdoor Discovery Program is a reason to reach out that isn't a sale
  • Tier progression: the Mastercard (5% Bean Bucks, birthday bonus, free returns) offered when suitability and propensity say so — a two-sided win with Citi
  • Cardholder activation: shorter time-to-first-spend and spend stimulation for new co-branded cardholders in the 12–18-month window that decides partnership economics
The margin question, answered per member

Industry benchmarks for intelligent offer arbitration: 20–40% lift in offer conversion and 3–5× ROI versus segment-based campaigns — because the discount budget is concentrated where it changes behavior.

For a base of roughly 10M members at ~$500 annual spend, a single point of churn reduction is worth on the order of $50M in retained revenue. We'll validate both numbers against your actuals in the workshop.

Real-world scenario

Post-service recovery: turning a complaint into a comeback

A long-tenured member submits a return dispute and rates the experience poorly. She has $15 in Bean Bucks that expire in three weeks. What happens in the next 24 hours defines the relationship — and whether those Bean Bucks are ever redeemed.

Without CDH

The members-only sale email queued for tomorrow morning fires anyway — the ESP doesn't know what happened in service. So does the “your Bean Bucks are expiring!” reminder. The member feels processed, not heard. Opt-out risk climbs.

With CDH

Both sends are suppressed the moment the poor rating is registered. A recovery message goes out instead — from service, in the right tone, with the dispute resolved. Once trust signals recover, the Bean Bucks reminder returns, timed to her. The relationship survives — and so does the redemption.

SHIFT 3 OF 4 — AGENTIC MARKETING EXECUTION

Maine weather moves in moments. Can your promotions move with it?

A cold front hits New England on a Wednesday night. Eight stores open in markets that have never seen a Bean Boot. Holiday, back-to-school and spring-outdoor peaks arrive on a seasonal clock with inventory that doesn't always cooperate. Your team shouldn't need five platform logins and three days of rework to keep up. Pega CDH makes the whole operation respond at the speed of now — with governance built in.

Agility, in L.L.Bean terms

  • Always-on outbound across email, SMS and paid media replacing batch-and-blast, synchronized with inbound behavior
  • Paid-media suppression of existing members so acquisition dollars go to true prospects in Birmingham, Nashville and Ann Arbor
  • Inventory-aware offer eligibility — stop promoting the parka you're about to sell out of
  • Message-fatigue governance — a cap on cumulative sends per member, enforced automatically across every channel

Marketing operations

One change. Every channel. Every market. Instantly.

Most retailers manage messaging across disconnected platforms — each requiring the same rules, segments and creative rebuilt from scratch. Multiply that by eight new store markets this year and 8–10 next, and the marketing team becomes the coordination layer instead of the strategy layer.

Why CDH is different Centralize rules and actions once. CDH propagates decisions to every member-facing channel automatically — with governance guardrails built in, not bolted on — so AI agents act within limits your team sets.
  • Weather-triggered promotions that adjust by region automatically — Maine and Alabama don't get the same cold-snap message
  • Seasonal eligibility that respects live inventory, easing markdown pressure on constrained SKUs
  • A new-store activation journey written once and launched per market on opening day — from first awareness to Rewards enrollment
  • Paid-media suppression of existing members, so lookalike acquisition spend reaches true prospects
Illustrative: one governed decision layer, every channel and market downstream.
Real-world scenario

The cold snap nobody forecast. The promotion that launched itself anyway.

Wednesday evening. A sharp front is sweeping the Northeast — 20 degrees overnight, first hard freeze a month early. Boots, outerwear and base layers need to lead by morning, for members in the affected states only. The window is 36 hours before the moment peaks and passes.

Without CDH

The campaign is briefed Thursday, built Friday, approved and live by Saturday. It goes to the whole file, including members in Nashville where it's 68°F and members who bought a parka last week. The moment has passed.

With CDH

A weather-triggered rule fires when the forecast threshold is crossed. Category, channel and member-level eligibility are already encoded — recent buyers suppressed, inventory checked, fatigue caps honored. Messaging surfaces simultaneously in email, app and on the associate's screen. Your marketer reviews a conversion report Friday instead of losing the weekend to coordination.

SHIFT 4 OF 4 — THE AI DECISIONING BRAIN

Your stack knows everything about your member. But what does it do next?

commercetools runs the storefront. Zipline runs the stores. Citi knows the cardholder. L.L.Bean Rewards knows the points. No one built the layer in between — the one that decides what matters most for this member, right now, and keeps every channel aligned on it. That's Pega CDH, and it completes the omnichannel investment you've already made.

Schedule the loyalty workshop →Back to Overview →

What one brain unlocks at L.L.Bean

  • Consistent recognition across the 60+ store network, llbean.com, the app, the contact center and wholesale
  • Seamless handoffs — an abandoned cart or a recent return follows the member into the store or onto the phone
  • Real-time next-best-action for associates and agents — a service resolution, a loyalty acknowledgment, or a relevant offer
  • Value Finder — surfacing underserved member segments to feed merchandising and assortment, not just marketing

The missing layer

Knowing your member is not enough

commercetools unified the storefront. Zipline connected the stores. Citi issues the card. L.L.Bean Rewards tracks the points. But none of them know what just happened in another channel — and none of them can decide what matters most for this member, right now.

Why CDH is different Other tools personalize at the message or segment level. Pega personalizes at the decision level — arbitrating between member empathy and business value in under 200ms, before any channel fires.
  • Evaluates eligibility, applicability, suitability and empathy simultaneously — for a promotion, a service action or a loyalty acknowledgment
  • Coordinates downstream channels so they act consistently — not independently
  • One centralized rule set propagates automatically to web, app, POS, contact center and partner channels
  • Completes the omnichannel infrastructure already built, rather than adding another silo
Illustrative: CDH as the decision layer between the systems that know and the channels that deliver.
Real-world scenario

The store that knows what happened online

A Rewards member abandons a $240 cart on mobile at 9pm — a canoe paddle and a dry bag. By 10am every channel already knows, and none of them act alone. She stops into a store on her lunch break.

Without CDH

The email team sends a 15%-off blast at 8am. The push team triggers a generic re-engagement at noon. The associate has no idea she visited the site. Three messages, zero coordination — and 15 points of margin given away on a purchase she was already going to make.

With CDH

One decision engine evaluates the context: what was abandoned, her Rewards history and points position, whether a discount is warranted or would erode margin, and that she's in-store now. The associate sees the cart and a suggestion: complete it today and the points clear her next $5 in Bean Bucks. One decision. Every channel aligned. Margin intact.
